That being said, it is also important to put virtual currency in perspective as a payment
system. The U.S. government indictment and proposed special measures issued last May against
Liberty Reserve allege it was involved in laundering more than $6 billion over several years.
Administrators of other major centralized virtual currencies report processing similar transaction

By way of comparison, according to information reported publicly, in 2012 Western
Union made remittances totaling approximately $81 billion, PayPal processed approximately

trillion in transactions, and Bank of America processed $244.4 trillion in wire transfers.
This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was
$1.6 trillion.

numeric.question: Compute the total volume passing through any detected cycle; compare to KYC declared monthly volume.
numeric.calculation:
1) Identify the detected cycle as the set of related trade-finance/supporting trade wires in transactions[0..3].
2) Sum amounts in transactions[0..3]: 189,493.08 + 17,606.04 + 14,542.60 + 9,590.35 = 231,232.07.
3) Take KYC declared monthly volume from kyc_profile.expected_monthly_volume = 57,258.0.
4) Compare cycle volume to KYC volume: 231,232.07 / 57,258.0 = 4.038 (≈4.04x).

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: Neutral: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting may be implicated, but the facts do not identify a covered financial institution or a SAR-filing failure/requirement determination.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates suspicious activity reporting by a covered “financial institution” under Treasury regulations when the institution detects suspicious transactions (and provides related safe-harbor protections). Element-by-element: (1) Covered entity: § 5318(g) applies to a “financial institution” (as defined/regulated under the BSA framework), but the fact pattern describes only Entity SYN_6f2f6999 as a convenience/grocery business and lists its outgoing wires; it does not state that SYN_6f2f6999 is itself a regulated financial institution (e.g., bank/MSB) or identify the financial institution that processed the wires. (2) Suspicious activity trigger: the wires are far above the declared expected monthly volume and include a note “trade-finance over-invoiced,” which could be suspicious, but § 5318(g) requires assessing whether a covered financial institution had a reporting obligation under applicable regulations; the facts do not specify what the institution knew, whether it detected the suspicion, or whether a SAR was required/was filed. (3) Conduct at issue: the question asks whether the described conduct falls within § 5318(g), but § 5318(g) primarily governs reporting obligations and protections for financial institutions, not the underlying customer’s wiring conduct. Therefore, § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting may be implicated, but the facts are insufficient to determine applicability as a clear yes/no.
